hook.text: For 300 years, economists assumed people weigh costs and benefits like calculators. They don't.

buildup.text: Expected utility theory says a rational person always picks the option with the highest expected value.

discovery.text: Bernoulli proposed this in 1738. It works on paper. But people routinely violate it in experiments.

twist.text: Allais showed people prefer a sure $1 million over a gamble worth more in expected value. We're not calculators.

climax.text: Expected utility describes how people should decide. Prospect theory describes how they actually do.

punchline.text: Rationality is a theory. Behavior is the data.

quiz.question: What did Allais's paradox reveal?
options: People always maximize expected utility
People prefer sure gains over higher-value gambles
Expected utility theory was never useful

hook.text: Two psychologists in Jerusalem rewrote economics. They had no economics training. That was the advantage.

buildup.text: Kahneman and Tversky studied how people actually choose under risk, not how models say they should.

discovery.text: Their 1979 paper 'Prospect Theory' became the most cited in all of economics. Written by psychologists.

twist.text: Economists resisted for years. Admitting humans aren't rational agents threatened the entire field's foundation.

climax.text: Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. Tversky had died six years earlier and couldn't share it.

punchline.text: The best economics came from psychology.

quiz.question: What made Kahneman and Tversky's approach different?
options: They assumed people are rational
They studied how people actually decide, not how models predict
They used only mathematical proofs

hook.text: Gaining $100 feels good. But losing $100 hurts about twice as much. The curve isn't symmetrical.

buildup.text: Prospect theory's value function is S-shaped: concave for gains, convex and steeper for losses.

discovery.text: The steeper loss side means losses loom larger than equivalent gains. This asymmetry drives most decisions.

twist.text: The curve also flattens at extremes. Gaining $1 million vs $1.1 million feels tiny. The first million matters most.

climax.text: This simple S-curve explains gambling, insurance buying, risk aversion for gains, and risk seeking for losses.

punchline.text: One curve explains a thousand irrational choices.

quiz.question: What shape is the prospect theory value function?
options: A straight line
S-shaped, steeper on the loss side
A perfect U-curve

hook.text: Before choosing, your brain simplifies options: rounding numbers, ignoring small differences, setting a reference.

buildup.text: Prospect theory has two phases. First, editing: the brain organizes and simplifies the choice.

discovery.text: Second, evaluation: the edited options are compared using the value function and probability weights.

twist.text: The editing phase is where most biases enter. How you frame a problem determines how it gets evaluated.

climax.text: The same gamble, presented differently, gets different edits and different choices. Frame creates preference.

punchline.text: How you see the choice is the choice.

quiz.question: What happens in prospect theory's editing phase?
options: Options are evaluated mathematically
The brain simplifies and organizes options before evaluating
People skip directly to a final choice

topics.title: Risk Aversion for Gains, Risk Seeking for Losses

hook.text: Win $500 for sure, or flip for $1,000? Most take the sure thing. Now reverse it with losses.

buildup.text: Lose $500 for sure, or flip for a chance to lose $1,000 or nothing? Most gamble. Same math, opposite behavior.

discovery.text: People are risk-averse when winning and risk-seeking when losing. The domain flips the preference.

twist.text: This is why people hold losing stocks hoping they'll recover, but sell winning stocks too early.

climax.text: Whether you're in gain or loss territory changes your entire risk appetite. It's automatic, not strategic.

punchline.text: Winning makes you cautious. Losing makes you reckless.

quiz.question: How does domain affect risk preferences?
options: People are always risk-averse
Risk-averse for gains, risk-seeking for losses
People are always risk-seeking

hook.text: Would you accept a coin flip: heads you win $150, tails you lose $100? Most people refuse. The gain isn't big enough.

buildup.text: Loss aversion means losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good. The ratio is about 2:1.

discovery.text: This asymmetry is hardwired. Brain scans show losses activate the amygdala more intensely than gains.

twist.text: Loss aversion declines for tiny amounts. Most people will flip a coin for $1. The pain threshold matters.

climax.text: Understanding the 2:1 ratio means framing gains as twice the size of potential losses to get a yes.

punchline.text: To sell a risk, make the gain twice the loss.

quiz.question: What is the approximate loss aversion ratio?
options: Losses hurt 5 times more than gains
Losses hurt about twice as much as gains
Gains and losses feel equally intense

hook.text: Students given mugs demanded $7 to sell them. Students without mugs offered only $3 to buy. Same mug.

buildup.text: Thaler's experiments showed that owning something instantly increases its perceived value.

discovery.text: The endowment effect: we overvalue what we own because selling feels like a loss, not a neutral exchange.

twist.text: Experienced traders show reduced endowment effects. Treating items as fungible weakens the emotional ownership.

climax.text: Before refusing to sell, ask: would I buy this at the price I'm demanding? If not, your valuation is biased.

punchline.text: Owning it doesn't make it worth more.

quiz.question: What causes the endowment effect?
options: Objects genuinely increase in value when owned
Selling feels like a loss, inflating perceived value
Buyers are naturally cheap

hook.text: Employees keep the same health plan for decades despite better options because switching feels risky.

buildup.text: Samuelson and Zeckhauser found a strong preference for the current state in all kinds of decisions.

discovery.text: Status quo bias: any change involves potential losses that loom larger than potential gains. So we stay put.

twist.text: The status quo often isn't a deliberate choice. It's what happened by default, and now inertia holds it in place.

climax.text: Ask: if I didn't already have this, would I choose it today? If not, the status quo is costing you.

punchline.text: Staying put is also a decision. Own it.

quiz.question: What drives status quo bias?
options: The current option is always the best
Potential losses from change loom larger than potential gains
People like variety

hook.text: You've watched 90 minutes of a terrible movie. You stay because you 'already invested the time.'

buildup.text: Sunk costs are past expenses that can't be recovered. Logically, they shouldn't affect future decisions.

discovery.text: But abandoning feels like accepting a loss. Loss aversion makes us throw good resources after bad ones.

twist.text: Governments continue failing projects for the same reason. 'We've spent too much to stop now' is the trap's motto.

climax.text: Ask only: what are the future costs and benefits? Past spending is gone. Only the path forward matters.

punchline.text: What you've spent is spent. Decide from now.

quiz.question: Why do people fall into the sunk cost trap?
options: They want to maximize future returns
Abandoning past investment feels like accepting a loss
Sunk costs are always recoverable

hook.text: A seller won't accept $450,000 for a house they paid $500,000 for. The market dropped. They still can't let go.

buildup.text: Genesove and Mayer found that real estate owners set asking prices based on what they paid, not market value.

discovery.text: Loss aversion in negotiation: concessions feel like losses. Each dollar you give up stings more than each dollar gained.

twist.text: Framing concessions as gains changes behavior. 'You're getting a premium location' works better than 'the price.

climax.text: Effective negotiators frame offers to minimize the other side's perceived losses. Language reshapes the deal.

punchline.text: In deals, framing beats facts.

quiz.question: How does loss aversion affect negotiation?
options: Negotiators easily accept concessions
Concessions feel like painful losses, making deals harder
Loss aversion only affects buyers

hook.text: A $5 coffee at a hotel feels normal. The same $5 coffee at a gas station feels like robbery. Same coffee.

buildup.text: We don't judge outcomes in absolute terms. We compare them to a reference point, usually the expected price.

discovery.text: Reference points determine whether something feels like a gain or a loss.

twist.text: A $60,000 salary feels great if you expected $50,000 but devastating if you expected $70,000. Same income.

climax.text: Happiness isn't about what you get. It's about what you get relative to what you expected to get.

punchline.text: Joy and pain are relative, never absolute.

quiz.question: What determines if an outcome feels like a gain or loss?
options: The absolute dollar amount
Comparison to a reference point like expectations
How much effort was involved

hook.text: A restaurant with five stars on Yelp disappoints. A diner with two stars delights. Expectations set the bar.

buildup.text: Koszegi and Rabin argued that our reference point is whatever we recently expected to happen.

discovery.text: Expectations form a mental anchor. Every outcome is judged as better or worse than what we anticipated.

twist.text: Under-promise and over-deliver works because it sets a low reference point. Anything above it feels like a win.

climax.text: Managing others' expectations is managing their reference points. Lower the bar and then clear it.

punchline.text: Set expectations low. Then exceed them.

quiz.question: Why does under-promising and over-delivering work?
options: It sets a low reference point, making the outcome feel like a gain
People forget promises quickly
It only works in restaurants

hook.text: Olympic bronze medalists smile more than silver medalists. Silver compares up to gold. Bronze compares down.

buildup.text: Medvec and Gilovich found that reference points are often social: we compare to peers, not to our own past.

discovery.text: Social comparison sets our reference. A $100k salary brings joy until you learn your colleague earns $120k.

twist.text: Social media supercharges this. Everyone's highlight reel becomes your reference point. You can never match it.

climax.text: Choose your reference group carefully. Who you compare to determines whether you feel rich or poor.

punchline.text: Your reference group is your happiness thermostat.

quiz.question: Why do bronze medalists often look happier than silver?
options: Bronze medals are worth more
Silver compares up to gold; bronze compares down to nothing
Silver medalists are naturally pessimistic

hook.text: Lottery winners return to baseline happiness within a year. So do people who become paralyzed.

buildup.text: Brickman's study showed major life events shift happiness only briefly, then adaptation returns.

discovery.text: The hedonic treadmill: your reference point adjusts to new circumstances. What was a gain becomes the new normal.

twist.text: This means more money, a bigger house, or a promotion produce only temporary happiness. Then you want more.

climax.text: Understanding adaptation means investing in experiences and variety, not status items that quickly feel normal.

punchline.text: You adjust to everything. Spend on what resists it.

quiz.question: What does the hedonic treadmill predict?
options: Happiness permanently increases with wealth
People adapt to both positive and negative changes, returning to baseline
Only negative events cause adaptation

hook.text: A shirt marked down from $80 to $40 feels like a deal. The same shirt always priced at $40 feels average.

buildup.text: Retailers use the original price as a reference anchor. The discount is measured against what you 'saved.'

discovery.text: The anchor price sets your reference. Every cent below it feels like a gain, making the purchase feel smart.

twist.text: Some retailers inflate original prices specifically to create a larger perceived discount. The anchor was a fiction.

climax.text: Ignore the original price. Ask: is this item worth this amount to me right now? That's the real question.

punchline.text: A deal isn't a deal if you didn't need it.

quiz.question: Why do strikethrough prices make discounts feel bigger?
options: The original price sets a high reference point
People can't do math
All discounted items are better quality

hook.text: The odds of winning the Powerball are 1 in 292 million. People spend $80 billion a year on tickets anyway.

buildup.text: In expected value terms, a $2 ticket returns about $0.80. Every ticket is a guaranteed loss on average.

discovery.text: Prospect theory explains it: we overweight tiny probabilities. A 0.0000003% chance feels much bigger in our heads.

twist.text: We're not paying for the probability. We're paying for the dream. The possibility of transformation has emotional value.

climax.text: Overweighting small probabilities makes rare events feel possible and common ones feel less certain.

punchline.text: You're not buying a ticket. You're buying a dream.

quiz.question: Why do people buy lottery tickets despite terrible odds?
options: They calculate expected value correctly
They overweight tiny probabilities, making wins feel possible
Lottery tickets always appreciate in value

hook.text: Which do you prefer: 100% chance of $3,000, or 80% chance of $4,000? Most pick the sure thing. It's worth less.

buildup.text: The certainty effect: we strongly prefer guaranteed outcomes over probable ones, even when the math favors risk.

discovery.text: Going from 95% to 100% feels like a massive jump. Going from 45% to 50% barely registers. Certainty is special.

twist.text: This is why all-inclusive pricing wins. Removing the last 5% of uncertainty creates disproportionate peace of mind.

climax.text: Certainty isn't always worth the premium. Ask: how much am I paying to avoid the last sliver of risk?

punchline.text: Certainty is a luxury with a steep price.

quiz.question: What does the certainty effect describe?
options: People always prefer gambling
We strongly prefer guaranteed outcomes over merely probable ones
Certain outcomes are always the best financial choice

hook.text: Going from 0% to 5% feels enormous. Going from 5% to 10% feels small. We overweight the jump from impossible.

buildup.text: The possibility effect: a small chance of something great (or terrible) captivates attention beyond its probability.

discovery.text: This effect drives both lottery dreams and terrorism fears. A tiny chance of extreme outcomes warps decisions.

twist.text: Insurance companies profit from this. We overpay to protect against rare catastrophes because we overweight them.

climax.text: The possibility and certainty effects are two sides of the same coin: we warp probabilities near the extremes.

punchline.text: Possible and probable feel the same. They're not.

quiz.question: What does the possibility effect cause?
options: We ignore small probabilities entirely
We overweight the jump from impossible to possible
We accurately assess small probabilities

hook.text: Risk aversion or risk seeking? Prospect theory says it depends on two things: gain or loss, high or low probability.

buildup.text: High-probability gains: risk averse. Low-probability gains: risk seeking. Each combination flips behavior.

discovery.text: The fourfold pattern: four quadrants of probability and outcome domain create four distinct risk attitudes.

twist.text: This explains why people buy both lottery tickets and insurance. Different quadrants of the same framework.

climax.text: Identify which quadrant you're in before deciding. Your risk attitude isn't fixed; it shifts with context.

punchline.text: Four quadrants, four attitudes, one you.

quiz.question: What does the fourfold pattern predict?
options: People are always risk-averse
Risk attitude depends on probability level and gain/loss domain
Only wealthy people can be risk-seeking

hook.text: You pay $1,200 a year for insurance you'll probably never use. On paper it's a loss. It still feels worth it.

buildup.text: Insurance eliminates a small probability of a huge loss. The possibility effect inflates the fear of that loss.

discovery.text: We're paying to remove dread, not to optimize expected value. Peace of mind has its own price tag.

twist.text: Extended warranties exploit this. The chance of breakdown is tiny, but the pain of losing a new phone feels huge.

climax.text: Ask: can I absorb this loss? If yes, you're paying for emotion, not protection. Sometimes that's fine. Know it.

punchline.text: Insurance prices peace, not probability.

quiz.question: Why do people overpay for insurance against rare events?
options: Insurance companies set prices too low
We overweight small probabilities of big losses
Rare events are actually very common

hook.text: 600 people will die. Plan one saves 200 for sure. Plan two: 33% chance of saving all 600. Most choose certainty.

buildup.text: Now reframe: Program C means 400 die for sure. Program D: 33% chance nobody dies. Most pick D. Same math.

discovery.text: The 'save' frame triggers risk aversion. The 'die' frame triggers risk seeking. Words alone flip the preference.

twist.text: Kahneman and Tversky showed this to doctors, policymakers, and statisticians. Everyone was susceptible.

climax.text: Before deciding, reframe the problem both ways. If your preference reverses, you're being framed, not informed.

punchline.text: Same facts, different frames, opposite choices.

quiz.question: What did the Asian Disease experiment demonstrate?
options: People always choose the safest option
Framing as gains or losses reverses risk preferences
Only non-experts are affected by framing

hook.text: 'This surgery has a 90% survival rate' and 'this surgery has a 10% mortality rate' feel worlds apart. Same data.

buildup.text: Gain frames emphasize what you keep. Loss frames emphasize what you lose. Each activates different emotions.

discovery.text: Gain frames promote caution and acceptance. Loss frames promote fear and action.

twist.text: Health campaigns use loss frames: 'not screening could cost your life.' Fear motivates action better than hope.

climax.text: Every piece of information is framed. The question is: does the frame serve truth or the speaker's agenda?

punchline.text: Frame shapes feeling. Feeling shapes choice.

quiz.question: When do loss frames work best?
options: When you want people to stay calm
When you want to motivate action through fear
When presenting positive news

hook.text: You won't pay $20 for a new movie ticket after losing one. But you'll buy it if you lost a $20 bill. Same loss.

buildup.text: Thaler's mental accounting: we sort money into separate mental categories, treating each with different rules.

discovery.text: Money is fungible, but we treat the entertainment budget differently from the grocery budget. Each has its own pain.

twist.text: Tax refunds feel like bonus money and get spent freely. But it was your own money all along, just returned late.

climax.text: Mental accounts simplify life. But they also make us irrational: paying credit card interest while keeping savings.

punchline.text: A dollar is a dollar, but your brain disagrees.

quiz.question: What is mental accounting?
options: Using a professional accountant for taxes
Treating money differently depending on mental category
Keeping exact records of all expenses

hook.text: Offered one coin flip for $200 or nothing, you decline. Offered 100 such flips, you accept immediately.

buildup.text: Narrow framing evaluates each gamble individually. Broad framing aggregates them into a portfolio.

discovery.text: Loss aversion makes each individual bet feel painful. But a bundle of bets nearly guarantees a profit overall.

twist.text: Investors who check portfolios daily lose more than those who check yearly.

climax.text: Zoom out. Evaluate decisions as part of a lifetime of decisions, not as isolated events. Broad framing reduces fear.

punchline.text: One bet is scary. A hundred bets are safe.

quiz.question: Why does checking investments daily lead to worse decisions?
options: Markets are always down in the morning
Narrow framing increases the pain of individual losses
Daily checking improves decision quality

topics.title: Hedonic Framing: Bundling Gains and Losses

hook.text: Getting two $50 gifts on different days feels better than one $100 gift. Same total, more joy.

buildup.text: Thaler's hedonic framing rules: separate gains to maximize pleasure and combine losses to minimize pain.

discovery.text: Because the value function is concave for gains, two smaller gains produce more total happiness than one big one.

twist.text: For losses, the opposite: rip off the bandaid. One big loss is less painful than the same amount in small chunks.

climax.text: Good news? Spread it out. Bad news? Deliver it all at once. This is hedonic framing applied to life.

punchline.text: Spread the joy. Bundle the pain.

quiz.question: Why do two $50 gifts feel better than one $100 gift?
options: People can't add
The value function is concave for gains, making two hits of pleasure exceed one
Smaller gifts are always better

hook.text: 'Get $5 off' works differently than 'avoid a $5 surcharge.' Marketers pick the frame that sells.

buildup.text: Loss-framed messages drive action when the stakes feel personal. Gain frames work for new opportunities.

discovery.text: Prospect theory is the hidden engine of pricing. Decoys, anchors, bundles, and discounts all exploit its curves.

twist.text: The $999 price tag anchors you below $1,000. The $19.99 feels closer to $19 than $20. Pennies move perception.

climax.text: Every price you see is framed. Knowing the frame doesn't make you immune, but it gives you a fighting chance.

punchline.text: Marketing is applied prospect theory.

quiz.question: Why is $999 used instead of $1,000?
options: It's easier to calculate tax on
It anchors perception below the $1,000 threshold
There's no psychological difference

hook.text: Investors sell winning stocks too early and hold losing stocks too long. Prospect theory predicted this exactly.

buildup.text: Selling winners locks in a gain, which feels good. Holding losers avoids realizing a loss, which feels terrible.

discovery.text: Shefrin and Statman called this the disposition effect. It costs investors about 4% annually in missed returns.

twist.text: Tax laws reward the opposite: sell losers for tax benefits and hold winners for long-term gains. Emotion fights math.

climax.text: Set rules in advance: sell when criteria are met, not when pain or pleasure tells you to. Rules beat feelings.

punchline.text: In investing, your gut is your worst advisor.

quiz.question: What is the disposition effect?
options: Selling winners too early and holding losers too long
Always selling at the right time
Holding all stocks forever

hook.text: Patients told a surgery has 90% survival rate agree more than those told it has 10% mortality rate. Same surgery.

buildup.text: McNeil's study showed that framing affects even life-and-death medical choices. Doctors are affected too.

discovery.text: Medical framing shifts treatment choices, vaccination rates, and screening behavior through gain/loss language.

twist.text: Ethical dilemma: should doctors frame information to guide patients toward better outcomes, or present it neutrally?

climax.text: Best practice: present both frames. '90% survive and 10% don't' gives patients the full picture in both directions.

punchline.text: In medicine, framing can save lives or cost them.

quiz.question: How does framing affect medical decisions?
options: It has no effect on patients or doctors
Survival frames increase acceptance of treatments vs mortality frames
Only uneducated patients are affected

hook.text: A carbon tax framed as 'climate action dividend' passes polls. The same tax framed as 'new tax' fails. Same policy.

buildup.text: Policymakers who understand framing design policies that feel like gains, not losses, for the public.

discovery.text: Prospect theory shapes voter behavior. Incumbents run on gains ('look what we achieved'). Challengers run on losses.

twist.text: Loss-framed policies often fail politically even when they're economically sound. Perception beats substance.

climax.text: Good policy isn't enough. It must be framed so citizens feel the gain, not the loss. Communication is policy.

punchline.text: Frame the policy right, or it won't get passed.

quiz.question: Why do some beneficial policies fail to gain public support?
options: The public understands all the details
They're framed as losses rather than gains
All policies eventually get public support

topics.title: Beyond Prospect Theory: What Comes Next

hook.text: Prospect theory is 45 years old. Is it still the best description of how we decide? New models are emerging.

buildup.text: Cumulative prospect theory, regret theory, and the query theory each address gaps in the original framework.

discovery.text: But prospect theory's core insights hold: reference points, loss aversion, and probability weighting still dominate.

twist.text: Neuroscience now confirms the S-curve. Brain regions respond to gains and losses exactly as the theory predicts.

climax.text: The best model is the one that changes how you see your own choices. Prospect theory does that better than any rival.

punchline.text: Know the curve. Then decide despite it.

quiz.question: What are prospect theory's most enduring insights?
options: People are rational calculators
Reference points, loss aversion, and probability weighting
Emotions have no role in decision-making
